Claude.notes: The Ken Olsen/DEC frame is one of the strongest openings in the catalog — it builds the control-vs-gatekeeper problem into a historical analogy the lesson then unwinds. The six-factor framework is well-sequenced and the Garante vignette gives it a real-world anchor. The lab is the only soft point: it is a reasoning dialog with an assistant, not a hands-on walk-through.
Claude.topIssue: The Lab 1 chat exercise asks learners to 'reason through' the six-factor framework with an AI, which trains the decision muscle but never has them actually touch Ollama or an open-weight model file — a missed opportunity for an opening module whose entire premise is that local inference is now hands-on-accessible.

Gemini.notes: Definitions of inference, open-weight vs. open-source, and quantization are precise and at the right depth for an Advanced learner. The Garante/GDPR narrative is directionally correct but reports the ChatGPT block as 23 days — the block ran roughly 29 days (31 Mar – 28 Apr 2023). Six-factor framework and tool-stack layering are factually solid.
Gemini.topIssue: The lesson states Italy's Garante blocked ChatGPT for 23 days; the actual block ran from 31 March to 28 April 2023, closer to 29 days — a small but checkable number that should be fixed before this becomes the canonical reference the quiz relies on.

Perplexity.notes: Written for the early-2025 landscape — Llama 3, Mistral 7B, Phi-3, Gemma 2 — and still relevant, but a 2026 learner opening this module will not see DeepSeek-R1, Llama 3.3 / 4, Phi-4, Gemma 3, Qwen 3 or Mistral Small 3, each of which has reshaped the 'what runs on a laptop' conversation in the last twelve months. The structural argument holds up; the examples feel one generation behind.
Perplexity.topIssue: 'Frontier models' are consistently exemplified by GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet; the open-weight landscape has moved on (DeepSeek-R1 in particular, released January 2025, is the most-cited local-reasoning model of the last year and is absent).

Claude.notes: The 4chan-leak-to-Alpaca-to-Vicuna arc is a strong narrative spine for the ecosystem story and the OSI 'source-available vs. open-source' aside gives learners the right conceptual tool. Narrative density is lighter than M1 (four story paragraphs vs. ten), which matches the more taxonomic subject but weakens the per-lesson 'story creates the problem' link in L2 and L4.
Claude.topIssue: L2 (Major Model Families) and L4 (Finding on Hugging Face) each open with a short scene-setter rather than a protagonist-driven story — the ecosystem survey still reads a bit like a catalog, which is accurate but misses the opportunity to seed each family with a 'why this model exists' micro-narrative.

Gemini.notes: Licensing coverage is precise: Apache 2.0 vs. MIT vs. Llama Community License vs. Gemma Terms of Use are correctly distinguished and the 700M MAU ceiling, Gemma's output-use restriction, and the OSI position are all stated accurately. Mixtral MoE numbers (46.7B total / 12.9B active) match the published spec. The Stability AI relicensing quiz item is a reasonable illustration but could use a clearer date anchor.
Gemini.topIssue: The lesson treats 'Llama Community License' as covering both Llama 2 and Llama 3; Meta's Llama 3 license is a distinct document that tightened a few terms — worth distinguishing explicitly so an enterprise learner reading this does not generalize the Llama 2 clauses to Llama 3 blindly.

Perplexity.notes: The family taxonomy stops at Llama 3, Mistral Nemo, Phi-3.5, Gemma 2 and Qwen 2.5 — all 2024 releases. For a module whose core promise is 'which open model family is right for your use case,' omitting DeepSeek-R1 (Jan 2025), Llama 3.3 70B (Dec 2024), Llama 4 (2025), Phi-4 (Dec 2024), Gemma 3 (Feb 2025) and Qwen 3 is a serious currency gap. 'Hermes series' and 'bartowski as primary quantizer' are both still accurate.
Perplexity.topIssue: Model-family table ends at mid-2024 releases; a 2026 learner choosing a model today would need DeepSeek-R1, Llama 3.3, Phi-4, Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 to make an informed decision, and none appear here.

Claude.notes: The RTX community-benchmark saga and the Metal GPU merge story do good work translating 'memory bandwidth is the bottleneck' from assertion into lived community experience. KV cache math is explicit, which is rare and welcome at this level. Narrative density is on target for Advanced technical material.
Claude.topIssue: The lab asks learners to design a hardware/software stack via dialog — strong for reasoning, weak for the 'did you actually look at your own machine's VRAM' moment that should ground this module.

Gemini.notes: VRAM-vs-RAM, FP16/FP32 byte math, KV cache growth formula, and Apple Silicon unified-memory architecture are all accurate. The llama.cpp CUDA merge (June 2023) and Metal merge (March 2023) dates match Gerganov's commit history. The per-tier GPU performance figures (RTX 3060 Ti / 3090 / 4090) are consistent with community llama.cpp benchmarks.
Gemini.topIssue: 'RTX 3090 at 1 TB/s' phrasing in L2 blurs with the 4090 context — the RTX 3090's memory bandwidth is ~936 GB/s and the 4090's is ~1,008 GB/s; worth splitting into two explicit figures.

Perplexity.notes: Hardware tiers (3060 Ti, 3090, 4090, M-series) are still the right reference points as of late 2026, but the module stops at M2/M3 and omits the M4 generation and the RTX 50-series (5090 ships at 32 GB VRAM), both of which materially change the price/performance table a learner would build today.
Perplexity.topIssue: Consumer GPU tiers end at the RTX 40-series; the RTX 50-series (notably the 5090's 32 GB VRAM) and the M4 Max are the current purchase decisions for a 2026 learner and should be at least referenced.

Claude.notes: Quantization is a notoriously hard topic to make narratively compelling and this module does better than most — the 'intelligence survives compression' thread is a genuine payoff. The GPTQ/AWQ/EXL2 comparison at the end could use a sharper 'when to pick which' heuristic for the reader who is about to click a Hugging Face filename.
Claude.topIssue: L4 (GPTQ/AWQ/EXL2) catalogs the schemes well but does not quite close the loop on 'given your hardware and task, pick this one' — the module gives information but leaves the final decision to the lab dialog.

Gemini.notes: FP32→FP16→INT8→INT4 arithmetic is correct, Q4_K_M naming decoded accurately (bits/K-quant method/size variant), and the GPTQ/AWQ/EXL2 descriptions match the published papers. 'Quality loss' discussion correctly cites perplexity as the usual metric and acknowledges its weak correlation with downstream task quality.
Gemini.topIssue: The 'Q4_K_M is the most common practical sweet spot' claim is still broadly true but the K-quants have been joined by IQ-quants (importance-matrix) for sub-4-bit, which should be at least named for a 2026 reader.

Perplexity.notes: Quantization is one of the more time-stable topics and the module ages well. IQ-quants (I-matrix, 1–2 bit) and the current wave of extreme-low-bit schemes (BitNet b1.58, 1.58-bit ternary models from Microsoft Research) are the newer threads a current learner would expect to see.
Perplexity.topIssue: BitNet b1.58 (Microsoft Research, 2024) and the IQ-quant family are now mainstream points of reference for 'how low can we go'; they are absent, which dates the Advanced-schemes lesson.

Claude.notes: Jeffrey Morgan's 'one command' origin story is a good anchor and the Modelfile walk-through gives the right level of hands-on content. The structural problem is the lab format: this is the first module where the learner is supposed to actually install something, and the lab is still a chat with an assistant rather than 'open your terminal, run ollama pull llama3.1:8b, paste the output back here.'
Claude.topIssue: The lab is dialog-only for a module whose entire point is 'install and run Ollama' — the capability delta the lesson promises ('you can run a local model') is not actually proven inside the lesson.

Gemini.notes: Ollama CLI (pull/run/show/list/rm), the Modelfile DSL (FROM, PARAMETER, SYSTEM, TEMPLATE), and the OpenAI-compatible /api/chat endpoint are all described correctly. The 11434 default port and localhost binding are accurate. 'Model files in GGUF format' and the Ollama registry mechanics are technically precise.
Gemini.topIssue: A hands-on module without a hands-on verification step: the lab asks the learner to discuss Ollama with an AI, not to run it. Even a 'paste your ollama list output here' checkpoint would materially strengthen D5.

Perplexity.notes: Ollama remains the right first tool. The lesson should at minimum mention the Ollama GUI app (shipped 2024) alongside the terminal workflow, and 'ollama cp' plus the OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions endpoint (added in 2024) are now part of the standard surface. Model recommendations in the examples lean on llama3 and llama3.1; a 2026 learner will run ollama pull llama3.3 or qwen2.5-coder instead.
Perplexity.topIssue: Example commands reference llama2/llama3; the current defaults a learner will actually type in 2026 are llama3.3, qwen2.5, qwen2.5-coder, and gemma3 — and the Ollama GUI (desktop app) is now the default surface for most new users.

Claude.notes: The 'LM Studio GUI vs. llama.cpp engine underneath' framing is pedagogically sharp — it teaches the stack by letting the learner see the same engine from both ends. Lesson 4 on llama-server and the OpenAI-compatible API is especially useful for setting up Module 8. Lab executability is again the pinch point.
Claude.topIssue: Same lab-is-dialog issue as M5: for a tooling comparison module, the lab should at least have the learner describe what their LM Studio or llama.cpp output looks like, not just discuss the tools hypothetically.

Gemini.notes: LM Studio feature description (model browser from Hugging Face, chat UI, local server mode), llama.cpp architecture (C/C++, GGUF-native, Metal and CUDA backends), and llama-server's OpenAI-compatible endpoint are factually solid. The GGUF naming convention mapped to K-quant tiers reinforces M4 correctly.
Gemini.topIssue: 'llama.cpp written in C++' is slightly loose — it is primarily C with C++ for some wrappers; the project explicitly markets itself as C-first for portability. Minor but checkable.

Perplexity.notes: LM Studio and llama.cpp are both current. The module should name the current alternatives a 2026 learner will meet: mlx-lm (Apple's native inference stack, 2024), vLLM for serving, and the ongoing shift toward structured-output / tool-use endpoints inside llama-server. The 'OpenAI-compatible' framing is right but is now table stakes rather than a differentiator.
Perplexity.topIssue: mlx-lm (Apple's MLX framework) is now the preferred path for serious Apple Silicon users and is absent; vLLM is the standard for GPU-serving beyond llama.cpp and goes unmentioned.

modules.module: M7: Prompt Formatting for Local Models

Claude.notes: 'Why the same sentence fails on a local 7B' is exactly the right problem to put at the front — it inoculates learners against 'local models are broken' when the issue is actually a missing chat template. The iterative debugging lesson gives learners a repeatable loop, which is unusually practical.
Claude.topIssue: L2 could do more to show the exact ChatML / Llama-3 / Mistral-instruct template strings side by side — the current treatment is good at 'why it matters' but light on 'this is what the raw tokens look like.'

Gemini.notes: The core claim — chat templates are model-specific and mismatched templates degrade output — is accurate and matches the Jinja chat-template specifications now shipped in Hugging Face tokenizer configs. Few-shot and structured output guidance (grammar-constrained generation, JSON-mode) is precise.
Gemini.topIssue: The lesson could cite tokenizer.apply_chat_template as the canonical mechanism — most learners who look this up will find that function name first, and it is the single most useful handle for the topic.

Perplexity.notes: Prompt-formatting fundamentals are time-stable and age well. The current frontier is tool-use / function-calling schemas inside local models (Llama 3.1+, Qwen2.5-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3) and grammar-constrained output via llama.cpp's --grammar flag or Outlines — this is where a 2026 learner will spend most of their time and the module could at least gesture at it.
Perplexity.topIssue: Function-calling / tool-use templates (now standard in Llama 3.1+, Qwen2.5, DeepSeek) are the single biggest practical prompt-formatting development of the last twelve months and are not covered.

modules.module: M8: Building Applications on Local Models

Claude.notes: A strong closing module that stitches the stack together: HTTP endpoints → prompt engineering → RAG → production patterns. The RAG lesson at this length is necessarily a sketch, but it hits the right beats (chunking, embeddings, vector store, retrieval, prompt assembly). The production-patterns lesson is the natural bridge to the next course in the catalog.
Claude.topIssue: RAG lesson covers the pipeline but gives learners no concrete 'here is the smallest working RAG with Ollama + Chroma + 50 lines of Python' — this is the one place where a code snippet (not just a dialog lab) would materially upgrade applied outcome.

Gemini.notes: HTTP endpoint shapes (Ollama's /api/chat, llama-server's /v1/chat/completions), RAG pipeline components (document loader → chunker → embedder → vector store → retriever → prompt), and production concerns (timeouts, retries, structured logging) are correctly identified. Error-handling patterns match current FastAPI/async idioms.
Gemini.topIssue: The RAG section defines the pipeline but does not quite nail the retrieval-quality failure modes (chunk-size tuning, hybrid search, reranking) that account for most production RAG problems — a learner leaving this module will know the diagram but not the debugging checklist.

Perplexity.notes: Application-layer content is where currency matters most and the module reads as mid-2024. Named entities a 2026 developer will reach for — LangChain's newer runnables, LlamaIndex workflows, Haystack 2.x, DSPy, Chroma/LanceDB/Qdrant as current defaults, rerankers (Cohere, Jina, bge-reranker) — are mostly absent. The production-patterns lesson could usefully name observability tooling (Langfuse, Phoenix).
Perplexity.topIssue: RAG and production-pattern lessons do not name the current open-source libraries (LlamaIndex workflows, DSPy, bge-reranker, Langfuse/Phoenix observability) that a 2026 engineer would actually install on day one.
